## Learning Objectives

- Explain the key components of generalized linear models (GLMs).
- For a given GLM, do the following:
  - Interpret the coefficients.
  - Interpret the results of a hypothesis test.

## Lesson

So far, we've covered three forms of regression:

1. Linear
2. Logistic
3. Poisson

They all fall under a broader umbrella of models called
"generalized linear models" (GLMs).
A GLM has two main components:

1. A distribution for the outcome, conditional on the covariates.
2. A link function connecting the expected value of the distribution
to the covariates through a linear model.

Let's examine how each of the three forms of regression we've covered
contains these two components.

- Linear regression
  - The distribution is the normal distribution.
  We assume $Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\sim\text{normal}(\mu_i,\sigma^2)$.
  - The link function is the identity function.
  We assume
  $\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}$.
- Logistic regression
  - The distribution is the Bernoulli distribution.
  We assume $Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\mu_i)$.
  - The link function is the logit function.
  We assume
  $\log\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}$.
- Poisson regression
  - The distribution is the Poisson distribution.
  We assume $Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu_i)$.
  - The link function is the log function.
  We assume
  $\log\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \log t_i$.

These are not the only distributions that fit into the GLM framework.
The other two most commonly-used distributions are the gamma
distribution and the negative binomial distribution.
Both are right-skewed distributions.
The gamma is continuous and the negative binomial is discrete.

Here are some graphs the negative binomial distribution:

```{r}
for(p in c(0.25,0.5,0.75,0.9)){
  for(r in c(1,2,5,10)){
    mu <- r * (1 - p) / p
    sigma_2 <- r * (1 - p) / p^2
    x_max <- qnbinom(p = 0.99,
                     size = r,
                     prob = p)
    barplot(height = dnbinom(0:x_max,
                             size = r,
                             prob = p),
            names = as.character(0:x_max),
            xlab = "y",
            ylab = "P(Y= y)",
            main = paste0("E(Y) = ",
                          mu,
                          ", Var(Y) = ",
                          sigma_2))
  }
}
```

Here are some graphs of the gamma distribution:

```{r}
for(lambda in c(1,2,4,8)){
  for(r in c(1,2,5,10)){
    mu <- r / lambda
    sigma_2 <- r / lambda^2
    x_max <- qgamma(p = 0.99,
                    shape = r,
                    rate = lambda)
    f_temp <- function(x){
      dgamma(x = x,
             shape = r,
             rate = lambda)
    }
    curve(expr = f_temp,
          from = 0,
          to = x_max,
          xlab = "y",
          ylab = "f(y)",
          main = paste0("E(Y) = ",
                        mu,
                        ", Var(Y) = ",
                        sigma_2))
  }
}
```

The default link function for the negative binomial distribution
is the log function,
meaning that with negative binomial regression,
we assume $\log \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}$.
The default link function for the gamma distribution
is the inverse function,
meaning that with negative binomial regression,
we assume $\frac{1}{\mu_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}$.
You don't need to memorize this;
if you type `?family` into the R console and press enter,
a help page will pop up showing all the distributions and their default link
functions.
(The one exception to this is the negative binomial distribution.
For some reason, negative binomial regression is not included in base R.
You have to install the package `MASS` to perform negative binomial
regression.
The function is `glm.nb`.
To find its default link function, use `?negative.binomial`.)

It's important to know that you can change the link function you use.
Although each distribution has a default,
it's not set in stone.
So, you can use the `family = binomial(link = "identity")`,
and your coefficients will be interpreted like in linear regression,
as risk differences.
It's also important to know that the distribution determines the relationship
between the mean and the variance.
With linear regression,
there is no relationship;
the variance can be anything, irrespective of the mean.
With logistic regression,
the variance is equal to $\mu (1 - \mu)$,
and with Poisson regression,
the variance is equal to the mean.

## Problems

### Problem 1

Suppose I own a shop, and every morning I measure the time between
opening my shop and the first customer arriving.
Let $T_i$ represent this time in minutes on the $i$th day of my study.
Let $E_i = 1$ if the $i$th day is on the weekend
and $E_i = 0$ if the $i$th day is during the work week.
I use gamma regression with the default link function
to regress $T_i$ on $E_i$.
My estimated intercept is 0.1
and the estimated coefficient on $E_i$ is also 0.1.
Interpret these coefficients.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

Our model is
$$
\frac{1}{E(T_i|E_i)} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 E_i \text{,}
$$
so
$$
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{\hat{E}(T_i|E_i)} &= \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 E_i \\
\frac{1}{\hat{E}(T_i|E_i)} &= 0.1 + 0.1 E_i \\
\frac{1}{0.1 + 0.1 E_i} &= \hat{E}(T_i|E_i) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
$$
This means
$$
\begin{align*}
\hat{E}(T_i|E_i = 0) &= \frac{1}{0.1} \\
&= 10 \\
\hat{E}(T_i|E_i = 1) &= \frac{1}{0.1 + 0.1} \\
&= \frac{1}{0.2} \\
&= 20 \text{.}
\end{align*}
$$
So, during the work week we would expect to wait 10 minutes
for the first customer to arrive
and on the weekend we would expect to wait 20 minutes
for the first customer to arrive.

:::

### Problem 2

Could I use a logit link with Poisson regression?
Justify your answer.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

This sounds like a bad idea.
For simplicity, assume there's no offset.
Then we're assuming
$$
\log\frac{\mu_i}{1 - \mu_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \text{.}
$$
If $\mu_i = 1$, the term $\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}$ is not defined.
If $\mu_i > 1$, then $\frac{\mu_i}{1 - \mu_i} < 0$
and the term $\log\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}$ is not defined,
because you can't take the log of a negative number.
This is really something you should only consider if your outcome is binary.


:::

### Problem 3


You work in Research and Development at Goblins, Inc.
You are testing the efficacy of a new potion on humans.
For each of $n$ human subjects,
you have measurements for the following variables:

- `potion`: The number of teaspoons (tsp) of potion
the human drank.
If this is zero,
that means the human drank distilled water as a control.
- `warts`: The number of warts the human grew after
drinking the potion.
- `green`: The amount of green in the human's skin
after drinking the potion.
This is a continuous but unitless scale
ranging from -50 to +50.
- `witch`: This equals 1 if the human turned into a witch
after drinking the potion
and it equals 0 if the human did not turn into a witch.
- `toad`: This equals 1 if the human turned into a toad
after drinking the potion
and it equals 0 if the human did not turn into a toad.

You have run four regression models.
These are the results:

```{r}
# Set seed
set.seed(8)

# Parameters
n_fourth <- 25e4
n <- n_fourth * 4
a_toad <- 0
b_toad <- 0.15
a_witch <- log(0.05)
b_witch <- log(2)
a_green <- a_witch
b_green <- b_witch
a_warts <- a_toad
b_warts <- b_toad

# Generate data
potion <- rep(x = 0:3,
              each = n_fourth)
green <- a_green + b_green * potion + rnorm(n)
toad <- rbinom(n = n,
               size = 1,
               prob = a_toad + b_toad * potion)
witch <- rbinom(n = n,
                size = 1,
                prob = plogis(a_witch + b_witch * potion))
warts <- rpois(n = n,
               lambda = exp(a_warts + b_warts * potion))

# Run regression
mod_warts <- glm(formula = warts ~ potion,
                 family = poisson)
mod_green <- lm(formula = green ~ potion)
mod_witch <- glm(formula = witch ~ potion,
                 family = binomial)
mod_toad <- lm(formula = toad ~ potion)

# Results
summary(mod_warts)
summary(mod_green)
summary(mod_witch)
summary(mod_toad)
```



Please answer the following questions.

#### Part (a)

For which of the following models do you need to exponentiate the coefficients
to get interpretable values?
Select all that apply.


(a) `mod_warts`
(b) `mod_green`
(c) `mod_witch`
(d) `mod_toad`
(e) None of the above.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(a) and (c)

:::

#### Part (b)

For which of the following models do the raw coefficients represent
risks and/or risk differences?
Select all that apply.

(a) `mod_warts`
(b) `mod_green`
(c) `mod_witch`
(d) `mod_toad`
(e) None of the above.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(d)
:::

#### Part (c)

For which of the following models do the exponentiated coefficients represent
odds and/or odds ratios?
Select all that apply.

(a) `mod_warts`
(b) `mod_green`
(c) `mod_witch`
(d) `mod_toad`
(e) None of the above.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(c)

:::

#### Part (d)

Which of the following models could produce impossible fitted values
for humans drinking ten teaspoons of potion?
Select all that apply.

(a) `mod_warts`
(b) `mod_green`
(c) `mod_witch`
(d) `mod_toad`
(e) None of the above.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(d)

:::

#### Part (e)

Which of the following models fall into the category
of generalized linear models (GLMs)?
Select all that apply.

(a) `mod_warts`
(b) `mod_green`
(c) `mod_witch`
(d) `mod_toad`
(e) None of the above.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(a), (b), (c), and (d)

:::
